context: Al-Fath is Medinan and came down on the road back to Madinah in the sixth year after the Hijrah, following the events at Hudaybiyah. The Prophet ﷺ had set out with roughly fourteen hundred companions to perform 'umrah, not to fight. Quraysh blocked the road, and after long negotiation a treaty was signed on terms many companions found bitter: no 'umrah that year, a return the following year, and a clause requiring that anyone reaching Madinah from Makkah without his guardian's permission be sent back.

That explains the surah's insistence on the word conquest. Nothing had been taken, no battle fought, and the pilgrims went home without entering Makkah. The surah opens by calling the episode a clear conquest and then spends itself showing what was gained: a pledge taken under a tree, hands held back on both sides inside the sacred precinct, believers in Makkah unknown to the army who would have been trampled, and a truce that made ordinary contact possible. The companions themselves understood the conquest to be Hudaybiyah rather than the later entry into Makkah, and al-Bukhari records Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib saying so.
name_story: Named from the first verse, where what happened is called a clear conquest. The word carries the sense of an opening as much as a capture, and the surah uses it three times, once for what has already been granted and twice for something near at hand. Calling a treaty that disappointed an army a conquest is the surah's opening argument, made before a single reason is given for it.

movements.h: A conquest, and what it settles
movements.note: The declaration, then forgiveness, the completion of favour, guidance and help. Tranquility is described as sent down into the hearts of the believers so that they would increase in faith, and the hypocrites and idolaters who thought ill of Allah are named.
The Prophet ﷺ is described as witness, bringer of good news and warner. Then the pledge itself: those who give their word to him are giving it to Allah, and the hand of Allah is above their hands.

Bedouins who did not come offer their property and families as an excuse and are told what they had actually assumed. They are warned of a call to face a people of great might, and the blind, the lame and the ill are exempted by name.
Allah states His pleasure with those who pledged under the tree and says He knew what was in their hearts. A near opening and much spoil are promised, which commentators identify with Khaybar.

Had the Makkans fought, they would have turned in flight. Instead both sides were held back inside Makkah, and the reason given is the believing men and women in the city whom the army could not identify. Against the zeal of ignorance, tranquility was sent down and the word of God-consciousness fastened on the believers.

The vision that started the expedition is confirmed as true, with entry into the Sacred Mosque in safety and heads shaved or shortened. The surah ends describing the Prophet ﷺ and those with him as they appear in the Torah and in the Gospel, likened to a shoot that puts out side growth and stands firm on its stem.

themes.t: A defeat that was not one
themes.d: The method of the surah is to rename the event and then earn the name. What the army saw was a return without 'umrah; what the surah sets out is a truce that stopped the killing, sorted the sincere from the rest, and opened the roads.

Tranquility appears three times, always as a thing sent down, on the believers at the pledge and on the Prophet ﷺ with them. It is presented as given from outside rather than produced by good news, which matters here, because the news was not good.
Verse 24 makes the withholding of hands, on both sides and inside Makkah, the deed of Allah. A fight that did not happen is treated as an outcome rather than as an absence of one.

themes.t: Who was actually in the city
themes.d: The reason given for the restraint is unnamed believing men and women inside Makkah who would have been trampled without anyone knowing. An entire military decision is explained by people the army could not pick out.

heart: Al-Fath is a surah about being told that what you lived as a loss was a gain. Recited slowly it does not argue with the feeling; it lists what was true underneath it, item by item, until the list outweighs the disappointment. Umar's objections on that day and his regret afterwards are both preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, which is part of why the surah is read the way it is.

Its second half keeps returning to what people were carrying inside them: what the bedouins assumed, what was in the hearts of those who pledged, the zeal that filled the hearts of Quraysh, the tranquility sent down on the believers. Read attentively it becomes a surah about interior states being weighed while an external event runs its course. It ends with a plant putting out shoots, the only picture of growth in it, placed directly after everything that had looked like standing still.

passages.why: A treaty that satisfied nobody is called a clear conquest, and forgiveness, completed favour, guidance and help are attached to it. Sahih al-Bukhari records that when it came down the Prophet ﷺ said a surah had been revealed to him more beloved to him than everything the sun rises upon.

Tranquility sent into the hearts of the believers so they would increase in faith on top of their faith. It describes calm as something added rather than achieved, and it arrived at the worst hour of the expedition.

Allah's pleasure with those who pledged under the tree, together with the statement that He knew what was in their hearts. This verse is the basis for the name Bay'at ar-Ridwan, the pledge of good pleasure.

The description of the Prophet ﷺ and those with him: firm against the deniers, merciful among themselves, marked by prostration, likened to a crop that strengthens its own shoots until it stands on its stem. It is the last word of the surah, and it describes a community rather than a battle.

connections.why: An-Nasr marks the entry into Makkah that this surah promised, in three verses, and its instruction is praise and seeking forgiveness rather than triumph. Read after Al-Fath, it shows what the truce was for.

Al-Mumtahanah legislates for the believing women who came from Makkah after this treaty was signed, which is the Hudaybiyah clause worked out in practice. It takes up the situation of believers still inside the city, which Al-Fath mentions only as a reason for restraint.

virtue.text: This is one of the few surahs with an authentic prophetic report attached to it. Sahih al-Bukhari records that when Al-Fath came down on the return from Hudaybiyah, the Prophet ﷺ said that a surah had been revealed to him more beloved to him than everything on which the sun rises, and then recited its opening. Bukhari and Muslim also record that he recited this surah on his mount on the day Makkah was conquered, with a quavering repetition in his voice. Both establish the standing of the surah and his own recitation of it. Neither promises a set reward to a reciter, and no authentic report does.
virtue.src: Sahih al-Bukhari for the Prophet's ﷺ words when it was revealed; Bukhari and Muslim for his recitation of it on the day of the conquest
